prompt.context: Office Vending Services Inc. (OVS) is the market leader in office vending machine services. The business services provided include sales and delivery of product, restocking of machines, and repair of faulty equipment. Profits are substantially down in the business.
prompt.question: The CEO of Office Vending Services needs Bain to assess the root causes of the profitability decline.

clarifying_info.q: What time period are we examining?
clarifying_info.a: The decline has been observed over the past two years (1996–1998).

clarifying_info.q: Are we focused on a particular geography or segment?
clarifying_info.a: No specific segment; the analysis covers the overall business.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have data on competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, additional exhibit data on competitors and market share is available.

exhibits.title: Office Vending Services Revenue ($M)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart of OVS annual revenue for 1996, 1997, and 1998.

exhibits.title: Office Vending Services Cost ($M)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart of OVS annual total costs for 1996, 1997, and 1998.

exhibits.title: Office Vending Services Volume Sold
exhibits.shows: A chart depicting the volume of deliveries/units sold by OVS over the past several years.

exhibits.title: Office Vending Services Historical Pricing
exhibits.shows: A chart showing average price per delivery for OVS over time.

exhibits.title: Office Vending Services Market Trend
exhibits.shows: A chart showing percentage change in market sales by player over the past 2 years.

exhibits.title: Customer Satisfaction (table)
exhibits.shows: A table scoring OVS and competitors on customer satisfaction attributes, alongside the stated importance of each attribute to customers.

exhibits.title: Customer Satisfaction (chart)
exhibits.shows: A graphical version of Exhibit 6 showing the same customer satisfaction and attribute-importance data.

exhibits.title: Competitor Comparison (1998)
exhibits.shows: A table comparing 1998 revenue, costs (COGS, SGA, Repair, Delivery), and implied profit for OVS, Vend International, and Candy & Pop.

exhibits.title: Office Vending Services Cost Per Delivery vs. Competitors
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of cost per delivery for OVS versus competitors, split into COGS, SGA, and delivery sub-buckets.

data.OVS cost per delivery vs competitors: OVS is 9.5% higher overall; COGS+SGA ~70% of OVS delivery cost vs ~50% for competitors; delivery sub-bucket ~half competitors

exhibits.title: Office Vending Services Cost Structure (Historical Trend)
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the percentage decrease in each cost category for OVS over the historical period.

framework: Revenue drivers: price per delivery, volume of deliveries, product mix
Cost drivers: fixed costs (SG&A, PP&E) vs. variable costs (COGS, labor, delivery, maintenance/repair)
Competition: pricing, service quality, sales/marketing, product offering
Customer: price sensitivity, attribute importance (delivery reliability, price, product variety, machine repair)
Market: number of players, market share shifts, industry growth rate

questions.prompt: What is happening to OVS revenues and at what rate?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note revenue fell from $250M (1996) to $230M (1997) to $200M (1998). Rate of decline is accelerating: -8% from 1996-1997 and -13% from 1997-1998. Candidate should ask what is driving the revenue decline — volume or price.

math.answer: Revenue down 8% then 13%; decline is accelerating.

questions.prompt: What is happening to OVS costs and is cost reduction keeping pace with revenue decline?
questions.guidance: Costs fell from $225M (1996) to $216M (1997) to $200M (1998). Rate of cost decrease: -4% from 1996-1997 and -7.5% from 1997-1998. This is slower than the revenue decline, so profits are being squeezed. Candidate should ask for a cost breakout.

math.setup: Cost change year-over-year and comparison to revenue decline
steps: Revenue declined -8% then -13%; costs declined -4% then -7.5% — costs not keeping pace
math.answer: Costs down 4% then 7.5%; not keeping pace with revenue decline, compressing margins.

questions.prompt: Is the revenue decline driven by lower volume or lower price?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 3 shows volume of deliveries is falling. Exhibit 4 shows average price per delivery has remained stable. Therefore the revenue decline is entirely volume-driven, not price-driven. Candidate should then explore why volume is dropping.

questions.prompt: What is happening to OVS's market position relative to competitors?
questions.guidance: OVS lost 20% of its market share over two years. Total market grew only 3%. Vend International grew fastest at 44%. Candidate should calculate market shares and competitor sizes from revenue figures provided.

math.setup: Market share calculation using 1998 revenue figures; total market = sum of all players
steps: Vend grew 44% — fastest among all players
math.answer: OVS holds 40% of a $500M market but is losing share; Vend International is gaining fastest at 44% growth.

questions.prompt: Why is OVS losing customers to competitors — what do customers value and how does OVS score?
questions.guidance: Price and Delivery Reliability are the top two attributes of importance to customers. OVS scores lowest on both. Vend International scores highest on both. OVS scores well on Product Variety and Machine Service/Repair, but these are low-importance attributes. This explains why Vend is growing and OVS is losing share.

questions.prompt: How do OVS's costs compare to competitors on a per-business-unit basis, and what are the profit margins?
questions.guidance: OVS's COGS, SGA, and Repair costs are roughly 100% higher than competitors relative to revenue. OVS's delivery costs are in line with competitors despite higher market share — indicating underinvestment in delivery. Candidate should calculate and compare profit margins.

math.setup: Profit margin = (Revenue - Total Costs) / Revenue for each player
math.answer: OVS has 0% profit margin; Vend International 10%; Candy & Pop 11%. OVS is operating at breakeven while competitors earn healthy margins.

questions.prompt: What does OVS's cost per delivery look like compared to competitors, and where is OVS cutting costs?
questions.guidance: OVS's cost per delivery is 9.5% higher than competitors overall. Within that, COGS and SGA account for ~70% of OVS's delivery cost versus ~50% for competitors; OVS's delivery sub-bucket is roughly half the cost of competitors. Exhibit 10 shows OVS has cut delivery costs most aggressively (-25%), which is harming the very service customers value most.

math.setup: Cost structure comparison and historical cost reduction by category
steps: OVS delivery cost per unit ~9.5% above competitors
Historical cuts: Deliveries -25%, Repair -14%, COGS -11%, Other -7%/-8%
math.answer: OVS is cutting costs most aggressively in delivery — the area customers value most — while maintaining over-investment in product variety and repair.

brainstorming.prompt: What are possible reasons for the drop in volume of deliveries for OVS?

categories.name: Competitive actions
ideas: Better marketing and sales efforts by competitors
Vend International entering new client segments aggressively

categories.name: Customer behavior
ideas: Customers switching to competitors with better delivery reliability

categories.name: OVS operational issues
ideas: Reduction in delivery investment causing missed restocking windows
Poor delivery reliability driving customer churn
Limited route coverage due to cost cuts

categories.name: Market/structural factors
ideas: Flat overall market growth (3%) limiting new client acquisition
New players entering with focused low-cost models

recommendation: Reduce product variety: discontinue low-demand product types to consolidate purchasing volume, lower COGS through economies of scale, and simplify delivery logistics
Reallocate spending toward delivery: invest in more drivers, better vehicles, and more efficient delivery routes to improve the reliability attribute customers value most
Work with suppliers to renegotiate or exit contracts for low-demand products; pass savings on to customers through lower prices to compete on the top two customer attributes
Train sales force to reposition OVS on reliable delivery and competitive pricing rather than product variety
risks: Existing supplier contracts for large number of product types may make discontinuation slow or costly
Changing the distribution and delivery network requires significant upfront investment and time
Customers accustomed to wide product variety may defect during transition
next_steps: Quantify which product types have the lowest demand and model the COGS savings from consolidation
Assess current delivery route efficiency and model cost of upgrading fleet/headcount
Identify supplier contract terms and timeline for renegotiation
Pilot reduced-SKU, higher-delivery-reliability model in one market before full rollout
